speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, October 3, 1983, consideration of Bill C-155, an Act to facilitate the transportation, shipping and handling of western grain and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Transport; and Motion No. 32 (Mr. Benjamin).

Mr. Speaker, yesterday I was explaining the problem that we saw in the position being taken by both the Government and the Official Opposition with regard to the amendment we have placed before the House. If Your Honour will recall, 1 was expressing my concern over the fact that once again the Conservative Party has joined with the Government to defeat what was no doubt in the best interests of western grain farmers. I was trying to make the plea, if it were possible, to the Conservatives to rethink this allegiance that they have developed with the Liberal Party of Canada, and to stand up foursquare on behalf of the farmers of Canada. I say it not only with a straight face but also with a very heavy heart, because as I look at the Conservative Party I cannot believe the duplicity that I see and hear coming from their spokesman.
Our intent, quite clearly, is to assert the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board over the movement of grain.
You intend to kill the Bill.

One of the Tories has mentioned that our intent is to kill the Bill. I want to make it quite clear that that is indeed our intent. I do not want to leave any doubt about that in the minds of anyone. I know the Conservatives want the Bill to pass, but we, recognizing the tremendous hardship that this measure will bring upon the grain farmers of the Prairies, believe that the Bill should not pass. In coming to that conclusion we have put before the House, on numerous occasions, the proposal that the Bill be divided in such a way as to allow the upgrading of the railroads and ports and to allow for proceeding with the disposition of the coal lands, while we could go on to deal with the question of how those things
should be financed other than through an increased cost to the farmers of prairie Canada.
I am sorry the Conservatives do not see fit to support us. I am sorry that they say one thing in Alberta, a different thing in Saskatchewan, something quite different again in Manitoba and a fourth different thing in the House of Commons. I want to suggest to them that if they could get their act together, it might be beneficial to the farmers of western Canada, rather than going around pretending to be all things to all people.
What we are saying is that the Bill as it now stands with the clause that we are attempting to amend would erode the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board. That ability of the Wheat Board to control the movement of grain through the grain car fleet is an essential requirement of the Wheat Board's operations.
We recognize that in 1979 the Conservatives attempted to erode that ability and they did in fact do so. But the Conservatives have been trying to shift that responsibility from the Wheat Board for a long time. That is to the detriment of the Wheat Board, the Canadian prairie farmer and our ability to export that very vital commodity as well as being to the detriment of the Conservative Party.
Let me suggest that without the control we are concerned about being in the hands of the Wheat Board, the block system would certainly be in jeopardy. The block shipping system is essential if we are to continue to be effective in terms of international wheat sales for years to come.
Frankly, we are worried that if the Bill in its present form is allowed to pass-given that we are now aware that the Tories will not support us in our opposition to the Bill-it will have a lasting detrimental effect. That opinion is not only our own but the analysis of many who are even more learned in the matter than we. Their opinion is that the future of the Canadian prairie farmer and his ability to grow and sell wheat for export markets will be placed in serious jeopardy. Because of those concerns we would frankly urge the Government not to heed the Tory support in this case, to pay attention to what we are suggesting and adopt it as part of the policy.
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this debate on the Crow Bill today. 1 have followed the debate with a great deal of interest and I have heard a lot of nonsense spoken on the subject.

The previous speaker?

October 4, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act

Not from the previous speaker but from some of the fellows to my right. I have heard a great deal of nonsense spoken and some of the worst was actually said outside the House by the new Leader of the Conservative Party (Mr. Mulroney), who implied in Saskatchewan that the NDP has come rather late into the Crow fight when we know very well that it is the Conservative Party that made the about-face in the summer and began to support us.
We in this caucus have been fighting this Bill very vigorously. That includes all of us in the Party whether there are large numbers of farmers in our ridings or whether we are concerned about the transportation aspect; it does not matter if we come from city or country ridings. I gave two speeches on transportation issues in June because transportation is a national issue, as agriculture is a national issue.
The effects of the Crow Bill in my riding are indirect. We know that if the Bill is passed and the rate goes up, farmers will have $1 billion less to spend. In turn, that will affect the people in my riding because they work in industries with very high lay-offs already. Consumer spending cuts mean that there will be more lay-offs. People who work in the textile industries will see fewer people buying their goods. People manufacturing farm equipment will find that farmers will not be able to buy as much. That industry in particular has been very badly affected. This is an issue for people all across the country.
The amendment before us today is very practical and is one that I believe we should all support. It is simply to ensure that the person in charge of grain transportation will be an employee of the Canadian Wheat Board. This amendment supports efficiency and good sense. The Canadian Wheat Board must control the shipment of wheat because it is Canada's wheat farmers who will suffer when the system does not work efficiently.
Let me quote from some of the testimony that was given to the committee dealing with this very subject. We heard from witnesses and members of the committee regarding the element of confusion with the variety of agencies involved in the whole issue, and we have a number of agencies overlapping authority and jurisdictions. The amendment is designed to reduce that confusion and to reduce, if not eliminate, overlapping in two Crown agencies. It will modestly increase and strengthen the Canadian Wheat Board. It has been the view of three Wheat Pools, the National Farmers' Union and a number of individuals who appeared before the committee that the jurisdiction for this kind of an agency should remain with and be under the Canadian Wheat Board. The Canadian Wheat Board, like any sales organization, must control shipment of its own product in order to ensure performance. For these reasons the Board has always held the view that over-all control of the system as it is developed, in co-ordination with the total grain industry, should be administered by the Board.
One wonders why, with this eminent good sense and the advice of the people most concerned and most knowledgeable about the problem, the Tories are not supporting this amendment. We get preaching about efficiency, we get preaching about good co-ordination from them, but when we come to a practical problem and to something that really needs to be done, where are they? Perhaps the Tories want to have a lot more confusion here. Why are they not after the most efficient solution to the problem before us?
Let me continue with testimony that came to the Standing Committee on Transport:
Today we are facing the very real possibility that the agency or a new agency with expanded powers and a powerful administrator will take powers away from the board and inevitably damage its sales efforts.
"It is imperative that grain sales and grain transportation not be separated", said one of the main experts who came before the committee this summer. The Canadian Wheat Board must be able to arrange transportation of its own product or it cannot fulfil its obligations to western grain producers or their customers overseas. The board's marketing success depends upon its ability to make day by day or even hour by hour decisions on grain movement. Its flexibility must not be compromised.
What needs to be done, Mr. Speaker, is very simple. We have had the advice of the people who work in the system. The testimony I cited just a moment ago is from a person who served as a Wheat Board Commissioner for many years. Why are the Conservatives not prepared to take this advice? Will the Liberals finally accept some sensible advice from the community they claim to be serving?
Let me continue:
We have a group of individuals in the Grain Transportation Authority and in Transport Canada whose abstract economic principles tell them that the grain industry has gone the wrong way over the past 100 years. They want to see the transportation system in a certain configuration and they except farmers, the grain companies, the Wheat Board and the Wheat Board's customers to adjust to accommodate it.
I suggest the reverse approach be taken. Let the transportation system develop to meet the needs of the people who are using it. That is the approach that makes real economic sense, and the Government should allow it to proceed by keeping bureaucracy out of the grain business. The Government has repeatedly stated that it will not remove existing responsibilities of the Canadian Wheat Board-
Yet it proposes to open the door to this by expanding the authority of this transportation agency. That is talking out of both sides of one's mouth, and it is not acceptable.
My Party will continue to work for amendments to this Bill. We want to see the Bill split. We want to see the constructive, productive parts of the Crow Bill go ahead, but we will certainly fight as hard and as long as we can on the parts that we do not want, the ill thought out parts, the parts where we have obfuscation and where there are inefficiencies right now. There is a great deal to be done to amend this Bill, and we intend to continue bringing in amendments to get a better Bill.
Of course we will support the aspects of the Bill that will provide jobs and improve the transportation system. Of course we will support those parts of the Bill that will enable development of the coal fields in British Columbia. There is good and there is bad in the Bill; distinctions have to be made. We will most vigorously continue to oppose those parts of the Bill

which will be damaging to the farm community across the country and will have a very harmful long-term effect on the rest of the economy, as a slack in consumer demand means a slack in demand for products made in the cities of our country.

Mr. Speaker, this is the fourth occasion I have spoken on what the Government is trying to do to the Crowsnest Pass rates. 1 rise again, but not with any great pleasure, because of the damaging effect the Government's proposal will have on the farming community and on the economic structure and fabric of Canada.
When I first became involved in the Crow rate, as most other Members from urban communities, I did so without any great, deep knowledge about the impact of the Government's measures on the economic fabric of the country. It was with the great assistance, deep knowledge and concern of Members of my own caucus, such as the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) and the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), that my knowledge and awareness of the impact of this particular Bill have been increased. They have done a tremendous job in the House in terms of representing the concerns of the farming community. Although the Official Opposition and the Government do not seem to realize it, the farming community plays a tremendous role in the economic life of the country. In fact, it is one of the largest generators of wealth of any group in Canada.
As the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) just mentioned, undoubtedly the measures proposed in the Bill will take away some $1 billion in earnings from the farming community. This will have a tremendous effect on spin-off industries which rely heavily on Canadian farmers for their livelihood. I know many people in my riding who work in such industrial enterprises as Massey-Ferguson. Undoubtedly they will feel the effects of this Bill. If farmers do not have the money, if they have less earnings to spend on the items manufactured by Massey-Ferguson, for example, then obviously there will be further cutbacks in the farm implements industry and there will be inevitable reductions in industries such as herbicide manufacturing and that kind of thing. It not only affects farmers in the country; it will affect consumers and people involved in industrial enterprises. The impact of those measures will be felt right across the country.
The intent of this particular amendment is to assert the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board over the movement of grain. The reason my Party put forward this amendment was because the Bill, as it stands, would erode the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board. The ability of the Wheat Board to control the grain car fleet is essential.
We all know that without control the block shipping system will be severely hampered. The block system permits the Board to ship grains of a specified grade or quality or a blend of grades and qualities to meet the needs of its customers. Without this ability, sales of Canadian grains for export by the Wheat Board could suffer. Certainly our competitive position
Western Grain Transportation Act would be weakened. Giving authority over the grain fleet to another agency adds an extra and unnecessary level of bureaucracy to the shipping procedure. This has been the experience with the Grain Transportation Authority since 1980. The movement of grain could be delayed by having an outside agency, without the day to day knowledge of sales and the grades, quantities and location of grains in storage, assume control of the grain car fleet.
The Wheat Board must be able to call the grain it needs, when it needs it, and be able to assign cars to the points where it knows it is stored. To fill this need, an outside agency such as the one proposed in this Bill could do nothing more than pass on the orders of the Wheat Board, unchanged, to the railroad. Certainly that has been the experience of the Grain Transportation Authority. This is obviously a useless procedure and it should be made clear that the board has control of the grain car fleet.
The House is well aware of the high esteem in which Mr. Justice Emmett Hall is held across the country, and of his inquiries into the medicare system and his authoritative knowledge of the Crowsnest Pass rate. Mr. Justice Hall appeared before the Transport Committee when it held public hearings in Regina on August 9, 1983. In his testimony before that Committee, he said and I quote:
The producers of western Canada are concerned about the ultimate fate of the Wheat Board. It is true that not too much is said about the Wheat Board in Bill C-155, but the beginnings are there and the capacity of the Wheat Board to control the grain fleet is being interfered with by the provisions of the bill. The capacity of the Wheat Board to control the wheat fleet is absolutely necessary. I hope the Wheat Board appears before you, and they will corroborate that statement, I am sure, because to meet a given sale the Wheat Board has to have grain, whether it is barley or oats, of a certain quality, of a certain grade.
I do not know, but if you went in, you would see that they have a wall there the length of this one which shows where all the grain in western Canada is and its grade. They have it so that they can call if they have a sale of so many thousand tonnes of whest of a certain quality; they know that it is either in the Regina district or maybe Edmonton or somewhere else. And to meet that, they are able to say to the railways that is where you want to get the grain this week and bring it to Vancouver or Thunder Bay. They have to be able to call the grain they need. If that were to go, it would interfere with the sales capacity and ability of the Canadian Wheat Board.
Earlier I spoke about the dramatic effects that the amendments which the Government is proposing to the Crowsnest Pass rate will have not only on the farming community but on consumers across the country. As my colleagues in the House have pointed out both during Question Period and in speeches on this Bill, there is hardly anything that the Government could even come close to calling a consensus across the country to support what the Government is attempting to do here. An editorial on February 4 of this year in the Toronto Star listed a number of things the Government is trying to do. I quote one part of that editorial:
Despite the opposition of provincial governments and of virtually every responsible farm group on the prairies, the federal government intends to unilaterally and drastically restructure the Crowsnest Pass Agreement. And if the Crow dies, the funerals of many western communities may follow . ..

As Western Canada sees it, the Crow is part of a Confederation bargain. Western Canada got low, fixed freight rates in return for agreeing to pay high import tariffs protecting eastern industries. Since then, the Crow's fixed rate-a half cent per ton-mile-has allowed our western farmers to compete for exports, from their land-locked position, with the transportation-subsidized farmers of Argentina, Australia,-
1 see that my time is up, Mr. Speaker.
Keep going.

My colleague suggests that 1 keep on going but 1 think it is sufficient to say that the Toronto Star editorial expresses the concerns of members of this Party, the concerns of farmers of the country and certainly the concerns that consumers right across the country will have once they fully understand the impact of the Government's measures.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be afforded the opportunity to join in the debate. As my colleagues have pointed out, it is interesting to note that the Tories do not have much to say here although they are frequently travelling across the country telling everyone how much they dislike growing bureaucracies. Yet they are, through silence and, I suppose, through their ultimate vote on Motion No. 32, indicating that they really want an increased bureaucracy. In a few moments I will deal with the reasons for that.
As our transportation critic pointed out yesterday, the Tories had 51 opportunities to speak on this motion on Friday and they chose to put up only seven speakers. I think that that really indicates what faint-hearted efforts they are making to support the western farmers who desire to see the Crow Bill scrapped and who desire to see that any changes that are made are in the interests of farmers.
The intent, Mr. Speaker, of Motion No. 32 is to assert the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board over the movement of grain. As it stands now, the Bill would erode the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board and that is certainly the view that is taken by one of Canada's foremost authorities on this subject, Mr. Justice Emmett Hall. Having read the Crow legislation, Mr. Justice Hall has concluded that if it is to proceed as it stands, not only will the farming community be dealt with rather destructively but the Canadian Wheat Board would be very quickly eroded.
I think that most farmers and most Canadians know that the Canadian Wheat Board was established in 1935 and had three key responsibilities. One was to market principally wheat, barley and oats, the second was to provide price stabilization for farmers for those grains which were held by annual pooling, and the third was to attempt to assure every farmer a portion of the available market every year. I believe that all of us in the House are now aware that the changes that would occur as a result of the Crow legislation would dramatically affect the movement of grain and the viability of many rural farms. 1 will speak about that in terms of the Kai Report in a few moments.
I would like to deal with the concept of the Grain Transportation Administrator for a few moments, Mr. Speaker. I think
most of us in the House remember that it was not too long ago that Mr. Horner, who was a Tory, crossed to the Government side in an attempt to achieve some kind of status that he was looking for. That move indicated at that time the Liberal-Tory alliance that existed on certain transportation matters.
I do not think we have to look too far into the Tory caucus to see who the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) would like to appoint to the new Grain Transportation Administrator position. He would probably like to appoint the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) and that is perhaps why the Tories are not speaking about this. The Tories say that they are opposed to expanding bureaucracy, but this proposal by the Government does precisely that. It erodes the decisionmaking authority of the Canadian Wheat Board by adding to it this unusual appendage. It is pretty clear that a Tory has made a deal with the Government side in order to take a shot at that job. If it is not the Hon. Member for Vegreville, perhaps Jack Horner, with the difficulties he is having with CN, is looking for another job to carry him on into the next decade.
It is imperative that grain sales and grain transportation not be separated, as is being proposed by the Government. 1 know that in Prince Rupert, one of the communities I represent, the present system is working very well. As a matter of fact, last year we again set records for shipments. Many Hon. Members know that there is a $3 million grain elevator being built in Prince Rupert right now that would perhaps be devastated by the proposed Crow changes.
The railways and certain individuals in the private grain trade, persons like Jack Horner and Otto Lang, I suppose, would dearly love to see more bureaucracy to allow for more high-paying employment for unemployable Liberal and Tory hacks such as themselves. The railroads should be set up to meet the needs of the people and the producers rather than adjusting its schedules and shipments for the convenience of the bureaucracy of the railroads and certain private individuals.
I mentioned a few moments ago that I would refer to the Kai Report. That is a report which deals specifically with grain production subsidies. I would like to talk about a few of the comments made in that consulting report in regard to this specific amendment. The report states on page 17: "Western Canadian wheat's international competitiveness is diminished by the relative generosity afforded the American product". The report points out that on average, U.S. wheat subsidies are $11.41 per tonne whereas Canadian wheat subsidies are $6.35 per tonne.

speechtext: Order, please. In the Chair's opinion, the Hon. Member's remarks are not relevant to the amendment at hand. Perhaps the Hon. Member could indicate to the Chair in what way his remarks are relevant, if in fact they are.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is pretty clear that if 1 am discussing what will happen in terms of the erosion of the Canadian Wheat Board because of the Liberal-Tory proposal
October 4, 1983

for a kind of subsidiary organization, I need to demonstrate why the Canadian Wheat Board is required to remain in its present and untarnished position without an auxiliary transportation administration. If this auxiliary transportation administration were to be set up, rural Canadian farmers would be negatively impacted by the changes in the Crow and would perhaps be less likely to be in a position to move grain. This is not only because another administration would be set up but because the cost of the subsidies presently in place in the Bill will make the situation that much more difficult in the future.
If you give me a moment, Mr. Speaker, I will demonstrate through the subsidies why it is important that the Canadian Wheat Board maintain the function of organizing what grains are to be moved and when, rather than have a subsidiary associated with the grain transportation administration proposal perform that function.
Western Canadian wheat earned 41 cents out of every grain export dollar, wheareas in the United States grain only earned 16 cents out of every grain export dollar. I think most Hon. Members recognize that the Government has made various proposals in recent years. For example, in 1977 a proposal was made in terms of the branch line subsidies. As of last year, those subsidies amounted to $278 million. As Mr. Justice Emmett Hall has pointed out, the federal Government was forced to introduce, even after bringing in a direct subsidy program, a branch line rehabilitation program which now costs us hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
I am saying that the Crow change will increase the cost of moving grain to farmers by over 400 per cent. If the government is to put this Bill forward as it now stands, including the concept that a grain transportation co-ordinator would take over part of the job of the Canadian Wheat Board, a great many rural Canadian producers will be negatively impacted because the Administrator will be making his decisions about what cars will go where and when, on what line and to what port, using different criteria from that used by the Canadian Wheat Board.
As I have said, the Canadian Wheat Board has demonstrated real expertise, at least in terms of the Port of Prince Rupert and hopefully in terms of the future of the Port of Prince Rupert. I feel that the creation of this subsidiary position will simply add another political, bureaucratic, decision-making body that is completely unnecessary.
A pork barrel.

That is right; it is simply a pork barrel.
The 1971 to 1982 average subsidy proportionally in Canada was 4 per cent, as compared to that in the United States which was 8.6 per cent and that of the European Economic Community which was 10.5 per cent. The United States and the EEC are clearly operating with a much greater level of subsidy to farmers.
As concluded in the Kai Report, the consequences of the unilateral changes will be to reduce grain production and grain
Western Grain Transportation Act
exports. I think we in the House must ask ourselves what kind of legislation would be introduced that would do that in a world that is already hungry for an export that is so beneficial to the Canadian balance of trade. In this trade, Canada exported over $6 billion worth last year alone.
The Crow change, Mr. Speaker, would take $1 billion a year away from farmers, an increase of more than 400 per cent by 1990. For example, this would have the devastating effect on farmers in British Columbia of a net drop in income of about 30 per cent. The addition of this supposedly beneficial position of Grain Transportation Co-ordinator would not bring anything like the long standing benefit that we have experienced with the Canadian Wheat Board. The Kai Report concludes that because Canadian farm income is lower and more variable, Canadian farms are less viable than their foreign counterparts.
On that point I should like to hear members of the Tory Party or of the Government explain how the addition of this bureaucratic position, separate from the Canadian Wheat Board, would in any way be of benefit to rural producers in the efficient and equitable movement of grain, whether to Thunder Bay, Churchill, Prince Rupert or Vancouver. From any of the evidence given at committee or any of the speeches made in the House, I have been unable to identify any way in which this would benefit anyone other than the appointment of some Tory or Liberal to this pork barrel position. It is of no benefit to the Canadian economy or the Canadian producer.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak on the amendment that a number of members of the New Democratic Party have addressed.
Before I begin my comments, may I say that I think the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) is not only very loose with his words but his tactics are very questionable when dealing with the truth. He likes to raise certain issues and talks about deals when he obviously has not done any research on them. Because he does not know what to do with the last paragraph of his written speech, he decides to put something in that he knows nothing about. He should get back to dealing with the amendment that is before the House.
The argument is always made by the NDP that they are the only ones to support the Canadian Wheat Board.
It is true.

They have certain hallmarks for those of us who come from the Prairies. Every time they hear the name, they have a Pavlovian dog-type reaction. Every time they hear the name the Canadian Wheat Board, they are for it and everybody else is against it. That is their first reaction, but nothing could be further from the truth, Mr. Speaker. They are so divided in their policies, so divided in their leadership and so worried about the next election that they have these knee-jerk reactions. We have seen that again today. The NDP has never

been in government in Canada and, with the actions they are taking, they never will be.
It must be remembered that this Party brought in the Canadian Wheat Board and this Party supported and defended the Canadian Wheat Board. The NDP has never had the opportunity to strengthen the Canadian Wheat Board. They have a good line of talk, of course. Those of us who come from the Prairies know that the ultimate reactionaries out there are the ladies and gentlemen to my left, the NDP. They seem to think that the only way they are going to get to power is to recall the 1930s. That seems to be their argument. They will rail against everyone.
Time and time again we see members of the NDP defend the status quo even though, through individual decisions, many farmers have gone well beyond that point. If we were to follow their line of thinking as the ultimate reactionaries, we would give ultimate authority for the right to move all grain to the railway companies. But the NDP members are always speaking out against the railway companies. You want the railways to have the ultimate and exclusive right of movement of all grain. When have you defended any movement by trucking? When has any member of the NDP done that?
We didn't tell anybody to carry the bags, either.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. First of all, I would invite the Hon. Member to address his remarks to the Chair, and then I would invite him to speak to the amendment.

As always, Mr. Speaker, I take your advice and thank you for asking the NDP to be quiet.
The amendment before us is based on very solid experience. All of us know that in 1975, 1976 and 1977 we were losing sales because we were not moving enough grain. There were bottlenecks. When the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) had responsibility as Minister of Transport, after extensive hearings in the country led by the Hon. Member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta), he came to the conclusion that there was a need to establish a Grain Transportation Authority, a Co-ordinator, in order that the cars be put to the best use in the movement of grain.
When members of the NDP spoke about this amendment, I never heard them speak of eastern Manitoba where there is a limited number of elevators, or where they are opening up new lines in areas where traditionally grain had not been grown. Some farmers have to travel 50 or 100 miles to elevator points at the moment.
What is the solution? What did we do? What have they done? They turned to producer cars. There is no question that in eastern Manitoba the Grain Transportation Authority, the Grain Co-ordinator, helped get producer cars. But did we hear anything from the NDP about that? They did not want producer cars and we must ask the reason for this. Then we get back to the ultimate reactionaries. In other words, that which
has not been done before has to be wrong because it has not been done before! That is the position they always take.
All across the Prairies we see farmers making decisions based on economics and common sense; that is a rational approach. They decide how they can become viable and remain viable. That is why I call the NDP the ultimate reactionaries: no matter how they twist and turn, they always come back to that which has been established as ultimately good.
In discussions on the Bill and the amendment I have yet to hear the NDP say how much money eastern Manitoba will receive from the $651 million Crow rate benefit for the maintenance of branch lines. I have asked them about that but they do not know.
All you need.
All we need! Have you looked at the branch line system? You will find that they are main lines.
You shut them down.

The $651 million is not going to be used for the main lines. Farmers in Manitoba happen to be some 400 miles away from the Lakehead. Should they not have the right to move some of their grain by truck? We do not hear about that from the NDP. Again, I say they are the ultimate reactionaries; every time they look at the reality they have what I call the Pavlovian dog reaction: every time they hear certain words they react in the same way. They do not look at the reality of the situation.
The point that has to be made about the NDP amendment is that, once again, that Party is willing to take the chance of having bottlenecks, of losing grain sales, of not moving grain and of reducing the alternatives. That, Mr. Speaker, is what they want. We will again have those long lines in front of elevator doors. We will again have a farmer standing there from the middle of the night to the next day, only to find out that the elevator is full and he has to pay demurrage charges. That is what they want, Mr. Speaker. They might not say that is what they want, but let me tell you that their position, their policies and their amendments will do just that.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I do not mind if they continue to live in the 1930s. I do not mind if they want to be the ultimate reactionaries. But I will not let them give this House and the country the message that that is the reality on the Prairies. It is not. What farmers on the Prairies want today is an efficient transportation system. One component was the GTA, and I say to the NDP that they had better start living in the 1980s or they are again going to be defeated as they have always been in the past.

Mr. Speaker, I lived through the 1930s as a young boy and I am very glad to know
October 4, 1983

that the NDP, which grew up in the 1930s, or at least they had short pants in the 1930s, have suddenly come to defend the Wheat Board. Who in the world originated the Wheat Board, Mr. Speaker? Why did they originate the Wheat Board? It was the Conservative Government that saved the pools, my friend from the NDP, so 1 have no apologies to make for standing up here.
I notice the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) taking off and the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong). All of a sudden it begins to register on them. They of all people should know something about the situation in western Canada.
You can make a lot of speeches in this House, Mr. Speaker, and as long as you are talking to a bunch of Liberals who do not have a clue what it is all about, as long as you have the representation in the NDP with only two Members with any remote relationship to the Wheat Board, then I suppose it is safe enough for you to say anything.
Our Party does not have that kind of representation. Fortunately, our Party has representation from rural parts of Canada and we are familiar with what has happened. We know what the Wheat Board stands for. The brother of the man who heads the Wheat Board is in my constituency, for your information, and I will be darned if 1 am going to go out there and talk against a voter of mine.
Oh, oh!

I know he has an impact with his brother. I do not care how you look at it, for us even to consider that he needs one more helper is an affront to him. I do not think he needs it. He is a very capable man, in my estimation. I think the NDP, in their valiant efforts to latch on to something, have come to the support of the Wheat Board. They have had to because all they have to latch on to is a few representations, a few farm organizations coming forward and telling them, oh yes, we need this and we need that. They do not have a clue what is behind the whole thing. But they say on the surface that yes, that is it. They have no research or no idea of what is behind the whole thing.
I know what the Wheat Board did for us, and I have no apologies to make nor do 1 stand here to condemn the Wheat Board. But I do condemn the NDP for thinking that all of a sudden, by their phony amendments, they can come forward and think they are going to strengthen the Wheat Board or make it appear as if the Conservative Party is opposed to the Wheat Board.
Phony amendments, that is right.

How can we possibly be opposed to the Wheat Board when we were the originators of the Wheat Board? If they want to take us back to the 1930s, let us go back to the 1930s and let the world know who it was that was responsible for the Wheat Board. You know, Mr. Speaker, that most of the social legislation was originated by the
Western Grain Transportation Act Conservative Government, contrary to what the Liberals have been telling us up until now.
Oh, oh!

They have been in power, yes, and as a result they have had the opportunity. We have heard all that. Of course, over a period of years, what can you do? But the fact is that the original thought came from the Conservative Party.
But no action.

You had better live with that.
Getting back to the notion of another employee of the Canadian Wheat Board-
The Board never even asked for that help.

My friend from Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) says they did not ask for it. Of course, that is because they are powerful enough as it is. So why are they trying to introduce an amendment which is supposed to do something but really does nothing? What do they expect one extra employee to do, overrule their friends? You really have to go a mile here to imagine what this amendment is going to do.
It does away with two bosses, Stan.

I just cannot imagine who dreamed up this amendment for my friend. Unfortunately he comes from Saskatchewan, but why would he even want to introduce that except that he was desperate for an amendment? I do not know where that idea came from, where it is going or for whom it is intended.
You should have been here yesterday and heard the speeches.
We are waiting to hear you speak. We have not heard you.
Mr. Speaker, I have one more minute but I wish the mikes were turned on for everyone of those 15 jabbering commentators over there.
There are only six.
I am sorry, I said 15. Well, they are so far away, and I am getting to that age; there are only six.
Tories never could count.

What is the point of this debate? It is just an exercise in futility. I think Madam Speaker should have ruled the whole matter out of order, frankly, because it does not really add anything of substance to the Bill. It is a waste of time even to discuss this kind of thing. Maybe that is what

Motion No. 33
That Bill C-155 be amended in Clause 17 by striking out line 6 at page 8 and substituting the following therefor:
(d) promote, and shall require, if necessary, reciprocal and other arrange-".
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the amendment is to strengthen the role of the Administrator to negotiate reciprocal arrangements between railroad companies. The important words are "to promote, and shall require, if necessary, reciprocal and other arrangements". The clause now simply states that the Administrator may "promote reciprocal and other arrangements between the railway companies to facilitate the efficient and reliable movement of grain for the purpose of maximizing returns to producers". The amendment would insert the words "promote, and shall require, if necessary, reciprocal and other arrangements". Again, the key words are "to promote a reliable, efficient and effective transportation system", but also in the interest of "maximizing returns to the producers".
I might point out that it was our Party that incorporated the word "reliable" and the phrase "for the purpose of maximizing returns to the producers". As I and other Hon. Members have pointed out previously, the mention of producers and the interests and concerns of producers was an absent entity in terms of the Bill. Therefore, this provision would put some teeth into the clause and give the Administrator the power to
demand, if it were necessary and in the best interests of maximizing returns to the producers, that he engage in reciprocal and other arrangements between the two railroad companies, or more railway companies if others are included in it. Therefore, it would be more than simply the persuasive powers that the Administrator now has under this clause if it were to remain as it is at present.
What are "reciprocal and other arrangements"? For the benefit of Hon. Members who did not sit during the course of the committee's legal counsel as "arrangements between railway companies", the most prominent type being that the railway of one company would operate over the lines of another company either for a temporary period or for the carriage of only one kind of traffic. He went on to point out that there are now occasions when there are voluntary reciprocal arrangements made, when there is a landslide or a rock-slide, but there is really nothing to encourage the use of reciprocal arrangements, particularly when one can move grain more efficiently in a more cost-effective manner. What we tried to do in the course of the committee hearing was to try to determine what sort of powers this gave the Administrator, and we found that it was really nothing more than simple persuasion.
Therefore, concerning the clause, I asked a question of Mr., Thompson, the committee's legal counsel, in this way:
I am trying to relate this to the movement of grain, Mr. Thompson. If this objective were to be fulfilled, would it be fair to assume that possibly you could see CP trains running on CN track up to Churchill and CP trains running on CN track up to Prince Rupert? Is that really what would be envisioned in this?
Mr. Thompson replied as follows:
No, in this proposal here the verb is the word promote.
He pointed out, "That is not binding, of course." I went on to ask:
But assuming that the word promote were removed and something more in the form of a directive were put in . .. that you could see the kind of situation that I just described?
He responded by saying, "That is right". Therefore, I went on to say:
-the word promote really renders that clause meaningless, other than that one could go through the gestures of promoting without having any residual power to enforce it.
Mr. Thompson replied as follows:
I guess it would be understood that the administrator would promote measures to facilitate the efficient movement of grain and among those some might, under certain circumstances, be reciprocal on other arrangements between companies.
I do not think this clause is necessary. I do not think it does any harm but I do not think it is necessary, because surely this is part of the kind of work that the administrator would do anyway.
What our legal counsel said is that it is really a meaningless clause in its present form. It has no teeth and no clout. What we are trying to do again, in our commitment and our desire to ensure that we have an effective, efficient and reliable grain transportation system functioning in the best interests of the producers, is to give the Administrator the power to more than simply promote, even though the NDP believe that the Administrator is really a nonentity. If necessary, the railways should be required to engage in reciprocal arrangements.
October 4,1983	__________________________COMMONS DEBATES
Throughout the course of the committee hearings we demonstrated the need to incorporate the necessity of maintaining producers' interests at all times. We moved amendments to Clauses 29(2), 18, 33 and 38. Throughout the course of our committee hearings we found it to be quite obvious that the Bill was written as a very favourable mechanism to the railroads. The major beneficiary in the whole Bill is the railroads. The benefactors will be the people of Canada, the taxpayers and, indeed, the producers.
We think that in every case possible it is important to inject the requirement that any efficiencies or economies of scale that can accrue must be incorporated. There must be someone to ensure that those economies of scale are brought about, because in this regime there is really a cost-plus system. Quite frankly, the railways will be paid for all their costs involving the movement of grain, and the higher the costs, the more they will receive. When there is this kind of cost-plus regime in place, we must ensure that there are some disciplines in the marketplace. Since there is a monopoly here, that cannot take place, so there must be some other monitoring device. Hopefully, the Administrator and the Senior Grain Transportation Committee would fill that role, but they must have the tools with which to do the job.
Of course, the whole business of an effective and reliable grain transportation system is brought about as a result of the production of the producers. As we have pointed out time and time again, they were the forgotton persons in this whole exercise. In amendments such as this we are trying to incorporate ways and means in which the producers' interests will be preserved. If we really mean what we say when we talk about an efficient and cost-effective system, we must use every mechanism to ensure that we get the best bang for the buck. As the Bill now stands, with the railways recovering all of their costs plus a 20 per cent mark-up for profit, it is certainly not in their interest to cut costs. It is in their interest to add costs. I believe these kinds of disciplines must be put into place.
I am disappointed that members on the Government side did not see fit to support this amendment during the course of the committee hearings. I believe it is a good amendment and consistent with what we should be trying to achieve in terms of establishing a very lean and cost-effective system. Unless there is the power to force the railroads to engage in these kinds of reciprocal arrangements which would serve the best interests of the grain industry and the producers, it will simply not occur.
I think the Administrator needs more than simply the power to promote. He must have the power to demand if it is deemed necessary and in the best interests of the grain industry and the producers.
I commend this motion to the House for support and I am sure that when Members understand and witness the kind of regime that we have in place they will see that it is certainly one small step toward incorporating some discipline which would hopefully accrue finally to the benefit of the producers.
